axioms: Legibility is a property of the rendered result under real data density, not of the list of techniques applied to produce it.

Visual channels (color, line weight, position) have finite discriminable capacity; asking them to carry more relation types or categories than that capacity holds guarantees perceptual collision regardless of intent.
A layout is 'stable' only if its coordinates are decoupled from the live data it visualizes; otherwise every data edit is a layout regression by another name.
Density reduction requires fewer visible edges or nodes by default, or a filter users actually reach for — encoding alone (color, style) aids discrimination but does not reduce count.
Canvas-rendered graphics carry no semantic DOM; accessibility for a canvas view requires a parallel representation, not attributes bolted onto a <canvas> element.
Any surface promoted as the primary or home view inherits the burden of working at full data scale on first load, not only in a drilled-down or filtered state.
failure_mode: Whether the underlying relation types and their semantics (inverse, symmetry, domain/range) are well-defined at all — this lens takes the data model as given and reasons only about how it renders.
Data correctness or contradiction issues in the source YAML — a beautifully rendered graph of wrong edges still reads as correct to this lens.
Engine/simulation-side authority questions such as cascade_edges vs. authored edges — those are data-model precedence questions, not rendering ones.
Content-authoring feasibility, such as writing 117 dated and far-future issues — orthogonal to whether the resulting graph, once authored, renders legibly.
Backend or pipeline architecture (build-time vs. runtime graph, validator implementation) beyond whatever data structure it hands to the renderer.
